description: Hi! We are Quantum Mind, a Baku-based team that loves turning space data into practical, creative ideas. We believe the best projects come from curiosity, teamwork, and a willingness to try something new, and we want to build something we are proud of during these 48 hours.
summary: Quantum Mind built an AI-assisted web explorer designed to uncover moving and variable cosmic objects within NASA’s SPHEREx all-sky survey. Because SPHEREx maps the entire sky every six months across 102 near-infrared bands, manually comparing over a billion objects for subtle shifts in position or brightness is nearly impossible.Our tool solves this by combining a responsive multi-band sky viewer with automated time-series differencing and machine-learning anomaly detection. Users can toggle between epochs, stack detector bands to boost signal-to-noise ratios, inspect live infrared spectra, and verify candidates against historical WISE and Gaia catalogs.   This project bridges the gap between big-data astrophysics and public participation. By making time-domain infrared astronomy visual, fast, and collaborative, we enable anyone with a web browser to help discover nearby brown dwarfs, comets, or distant planets
details:
What it does

Challenge asks for

In the tool

Enter RA and Dec, see a series of images "like a little video"

Coordinates in degrees or h:m:s, or an object name. Epoch blink plays one deep image per SPHEREx visit; Exposure movie plays every single exposure.

Easy to update with new data releases

python tools/build_index.py re-reads the public bucket and adds new exposures. Finished periods are cached.

Use the 102 bands; add the data of each of the six detectors; spectra on the fly

Buttons 1–6 add the exposures of one detector. Click any point: its 102-channel spectrum is measured from the loaded exposures, one colour per epoch, downloadable as CSV.

Add or subtract images taken at different times

Difference view: one epoch minus another. Fixed stars cancel; a moving star shows as a white-black pair.

Let users choose the field of view

2 to 16 arcmin.

Overlay Gaia or WISE

Gaia DR3 stars (moved to the date of each frame with their proper motion) and CatWISE2020 sources.

Coordinates in the URL

?ra=133.7951&dec=-7.2451&fov=6&depth=6&view=epochs&det=6 reopens any view; "Copy link" gives it.

Show metadata

Per-exposure panel: observation id, release, time, detector, wavelength, exposure time, sky level, noise, link to the FITS file.

"…even new planets reveal themselves by shifting position"

Planet X stack: removes the fixed sky and shift-and-stacks one visit along the track of a body at a chosen distance from the Sun. It can scan all distances and inject a test planet.

Tested on the challenge targets

Screenshots are in figures/: Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, Pluto, Eris and the Planet 9 zone (the Epsilon Indi B and WISE 0855 ones come from an earlier build of the same day). bash tools/make_figures.sh re-captures all presets.

Target

What the tool shows

Barnard's Star

Difference of the 2026 and 2025 epochs gives a clear north-south white-black pair: the star moved north, as its 10.4 arcsec/yr proper motion predicts. The star saturates below 3.8 µm; at 4–5 µm the spectrum reads 2–4 Jy.

Epsilon Indi B

The brown-dwarf pair moves south-east between epochs. The spectrum (20–45 mJy) shows the peaks near 1.3, 1.6, 2.1 and 4.1 µm and the deep methane and water absorption between them, the same in all four epochs.

WISE 0855

Too faint for single exposures. At its predicted position the spectrum has a 4.4–5 µm excess of about 0.5 mJy, which matches its known brightness (W2 = 13.9 mag). At this date it is blended with a background star that dominates below 3 µm.

RW Aurigae, R Draconis

Both open as presets from pre-downloaded cutouts (333 and 354 exposures). The spectrum panel colours each epoch separately, so brightness changes between visits can be compared. Not yet inspected by us: open both once and record what they show before quoting a result.

Planet X: what the stack can and cannot do

Validation on bodies whose position is known (ephemeris from JPL Horizons through IRSA's moving-object search):

Test

Result

Pluto, April 2026 visit (98 exposures)

Found at 449 σ. Best-fit distance 36 AU (true 35.5 AU). Position 1 arcsec from the ephemeris.

Eris, July 2025 visit (112 exposures; V = 18.7, 96 AU)

Found at 13 σ, 2 arcsec from the ephemeris. It is hard to see in any single exposure. Its best-fit circular-orbit distance is 144 AU: Eris is near the far end of an eccentric orbit and moves slower than a circular orbit would.

Same fields, epochs without the body

Brightest point 5–8 σ. We therefore treat only peaks of 9 σ or more as signals.

Injected test planets, Taurus field (RA 60°, Dec +20°), detectors 1–2, one visit, 36 exposures

200 µJy (AB 18.2): recovered at 21–23 σ. 100 µJy (AB 18.9): recovered at 10.4 σ. 60 µJy (AB 19.5): not recovered.

So one visit reaches about AB 19.0 (about 90 µJy at 0.75–1.6 µm). In that pilot field no signal above 9 σ was found.

Where the numbers come from: the Pluto and Eris rows are the printed output of node tools/planetx.mjs pack pluto and ... pack eris; the injection rows are also saved in results/planetx.jsonl. Re-run the two commands to append the Pluto and Eris rows to that file.

What this means for Planet Nine (Brown & Batygin 2021; Brown, Holman & Batygin 2024): the models that optical surveys have not yet excluded have V ≈ 22 at about 550 AU, which is 2–3 magnitudes fainter than one SPHEREx visit reaches. With the data public today the tool can find a Neptune-size, highly reflective planet out to roughly 480 AU, and smaller, nearer bodies such as Eris. We claim no discovery. The tool makes the search possible for anyone, and the limit improves as SPHEREx repeats its survey.

Known limits of the method:

  • The stack assumes a circular orbit. Beyond about 300 AU a body barely moves within one visit, so its distance has to come from finding it again in another epoch; the tool lists where to look.
  • A bright body passing through the field (Pluto) can leave a faint trace in the stacks of visits with few exposures.
  • The pixel-flag layer of the SPHEREx files is compressed and cannot be read piece by piece from a browser. The tool rejects dead and hot pixels itself and uses a trimmed mean when adding exposures.
  • Fluxes are aperture photometry (9 arcsec radius) without aperture correction; treat them as good to about 10–20 %.

How it works

tools/build_index.py ──► docs/index/ (4,584 small JSON files: 1,628,230 images, where each one points)
│
browser ── RA, Dec ────────────►│ which exposures cover this point?
── HTTP range requests ─────────► NASA SPHEREx bucket on Amazon S3
35 kB header (pointing) s3://nasa-irsa-spherex (public, CORS enabled)
+ only the detector rows needed (0.4–1 MB instead of 65 MB per image)
── resample north-up, subtract sky, stack, difference, photometry, shift-and-stack

  • No server. IRSA's search services cannot be called from a web page (no CORS) and were overloaded during the hackathon. The tool needs only the S3 bucket and its own static index.
  • Index. One 1 kB header slice per exposure gives the pointing of detector 1; the other five detectors follow from the fixed focal-plane geometry (measured to 0.006°). The page confirms every hit with the real header.
  • Astrometry. TAN projection with SIP distortion, written in JavaScript and checked against astropy: positions agree to 10⁻⁹ pixel, wavelengths to 5×10⁻⁷ µm (node tests/test_core.mjs). Gaia stars land on the SPHEREx stars.
  • Wavelength. SPHEREx filters change colour across each detector, so every exposure sees a different wavelength at a given sky point. The page reads it from the mission's lookup table (docs/wave.json).
  • Planet X stack. Fixed sky = per-pixel median of all exposures of a detector, bright stars masked. Track = parallax from the Earth's orbit plus a circular orbit at the trial distance and tilt. Exposures are shifted along the track and added with a trimmed mean; the result is a signal-to-noise map.
  • Packs. The preset targets ship pre-downloaded cutouts (docs/packs/) so they open at once on a slow network. Any other position is downloaded live.
